final.title: Why stopping rules are not enough in small-business workflows
final.body:
Stopping rules sound neat until you meet the real workflow. In a small business, the problem is usually not the first rule. It is the exception: the invoice that is over the usual amount, the customer record that is incomplete, the lead that looks promising but needs a human eye. A simple if-then rule can stop work, but it can also stop the wrong work or let the wrong thing through. That is why a bounded automation decision should start with the exception path, not the happy path.

The practical question is simple: in your repeated workflow, what judgment calls keep showing up that a fixed rule would miss? If the answer is “almost none,” AI probably is not worth the trouble. If the answer is “quite a few,” map those exceptions on one page. Mark which ones can be checked automatically, which ones should be routed to a person, and which ones must never be auto-approved.

That distinction matters most where money is involved. Human approval stays in place for payments and other high-risk decisions. In Bareni’s self-built accounts-payable demo, amount-based human-only approval and blocked payment attempts were shown on synthetic data; that is a demo boundary, not a customer result. The system can flag, sort, and prepare work. It should not quietly decide on the risky bit.

If your workflow already lives in digital documents and SaaS tools, that one-page exception map is the right starting point. It gives you a plain decision: keep it manual, hire for it, or automate only the parts that do not need judgment. The cost of one wrong rule can be boringly expensive.
